attacks.claim: The compiled-in minisign key has no rotation, revocation, or key-ID handling. A leaked key lets forged archives verify on every installed binary, and the only recovery channel is the compromised one.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: key rotation, revocation, or key-ID handling. Quote: 'The minisign public key is compiled into the binary; the archive is rejected unless the signature verifies.'

attacks.claim: Neither the latest-tag query nor --version has an anti-downgrade or minimum-version guard, so a validly signed older release with a known flaw can be installed. This works against the plan's own goal of moving users off old versions.
attacks.evidence: 'kvx self-update [--check] [--version vX.Y.Z]' and 'Queries the GitHub Releases API for the latest non-prerelease tag'; ABSENT: anti-downgrade policy.

attacks.claim: There is no post-replace verification and no automatic rollback. A correctly signed but broken or wrong-platform archive leaves the user with a broken kvx and a manual --rollback step.
attacks.evidence: 'atomic rename over the current binary'; ABSENT: post-install smoke test or automatic rollback on failure.

attacks.claim: The replace sequence does not cover a crash between the rename and the kvx.prev write, or a stale kvx.prev left by an earlier update. The test list has no crash-during-update case.
attacks.evidence: 'The previous binary is kept as kvx.prev'; testing list covers only valid signature, bad signature, truncated download, non-writable directory, rollback, and refusal paths.

attacks.claim: kvx.prev holds one prior binary and is overwritten on each update. A second bad release removes the working rollback target, and the retention rule is unstated.
attacks.evidence: 'The previous binary is kept as kvx.prev; kvx self-update --rollback swaps them back.'

attacks.claim: Package-manager refusal is path-based only. Symlinks such as /usr/local/bin/kvx into a Cellar are not resolved, and the rpm ownership method is unstated (rpm does not use the dpkg database), so the check can overwrite managed files or refuse valid standalone installs.
attacks.evidence: 'if the binary path is under a Homebrew Cellar or is owned by the dpkg/rpm database, self-update refuses'; ABSENT: symlink resolution and rpm detection method.

attacks.claim: Every POST exposes the client IP to the donated VPS web server, and its access logs are not addressed. The 'discarded after aggregation' claim covers only raw events, so the data-minimisation promise does not hold end to end.
attacks.evidence: 'writing daily aggregate counts only (raw events discarded after aggregation)'; ABSENT: client-IP handling or access-log retention.

attacks.claim: The persistent random install ID makes installs linkable across days when joined with version and OS/arch. Its lifecycle (rotation, deletion on telemetry off, server-side retention) is unstated.
attacks.evidence: 'a random install ID generated locally (not derived from hostname, user, or MAC)'; ABSENT: rotation, deletion on opt-out, or retention.

attacks.claim: The consent prompt calls the data 'anonymous', but the payload includes a persistent install ID, and the prompt omits the ID, the collector, and retention. This does not match the agreed explicit-consent constraint, because users are not told what they are agreeing to.
attacks.evidence: 'Share anonymous usage stats (command name, backend type, kvx version, OS/arch)? [y/N]'; payload includes 'a random install ID generated locally'.

attacks.claim: A persistent pseudonymous ID is personal data under GDPR-style regimes. The plan gives no lawful basis, controller identity, privacy notice, or data-subject request path, and no stored consent record.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: lawful basis, controller, jurisdiction, privacy notice, data-subject request process, consent record.

attacks.claim: The 41% figure counts release-asset downloads, which include mirrors, CI, and Homebrew fetches. It does not measure installed versions, and the 59% baseline has no derivation, so the 75% target cannot be verified.
attacks.evidence: '41% of release-asset downloads 60 days later were still for versions <= v2.6.2 (GitHub release download counts, tallied per asset)' and '(from 59%)'; ABSENT: method linking downloads to installed versions.

attacks.claim: Opt-in telemetry from a default-off prompt will over-represent engaged users, yet the plan uses it to set backend priorities. No expected opt-in rate, sample-size estimate, or bias check is stated.
attacks.evidence: 'Backend prioritisation is currently guesswork' and 'Telemetry opt-in rate reported transparently in stats/; no target'.

attacks.claim: Two maintainers must deliver self-update with rollback, package-manager detection, the notice, the telemetry client, the consent flow, a deployed collector, docs, and an RC soak in 3 weeks. Week 3 has no slack, and telemetry is not needed to ship self-update, so the two should be decoupled.
attacks.evidence: 'Week 3: collector service, docs/telemetry.md, release notes, v2.8.0-rc1 for 1 week, then v2.8.0.'

attacks.claim: The default-on update check sends the client IP and user agent to GitHub every 24 h. The plan does not state this in the docs or consent scope.
attacks.evidence: 'single HTTPS GET with a 1.5 s timeout'; ABSENT: disclosure of what the update check sends.

attacks.claim: The plan does not say when the install ID is generated relative to the consent answer. If it is created before consent, data is stored before the user agrees.
attacks.evidence: 'a random install ID generated locally'; ABSENT: generation timing relative to the consent prompt.

attacks.claim: Opt-out is not retroactive, and the plan gives no deletion or retraction process for received events or already-published stats/ aggregates.
attacks.evidence: 'Changeable any time: kvx telemetry on|off|status'; ABSENT: deletion semantics on opt-out or retraction of published stats.

attacks.claim: The payload has no schema version field, so later schema changes will break comparison with historical aggregates.
attacks.evidence: Payload list has no schema version; 'Aggregates are published monthly in the repo under stats/.'

attacks.claim: User-supplied --version and release tag strings are not validated before use in download URLs or temp-file paths.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: input validation for --version and tag names.

attacks.claim: Telemetry failures are dropped silently with no health metric, so a broken collector or schema bug would go unnoticed while release notes say data is collected.
attacks.evidence: 'failures are dropped, never retried in the foreground'; ABSENT: health metric or alerting.

attacks.claim: The goroutine for the update check or POST has no stated teardown when the command exits, which can truncate output or delay short commands.
attacks.evidence: 'run in a goroutine; it never delays the command'; ABSENT: teardown on exit.

attacks.claim: Update discovery depends on GitHub and telemetry on a single donated VPS, with no fallback, self-hosted collector option, or exit plan if the donation ends.
attacks.evidence: 'on the project's existing donated VPS' and 'Queries the GitHub Releases API'; ABSENT: fallback or exit plan.

attacks.claim: There is no load or capacity estimate for daily POSTs to the collector, no rate limit or backpressure, and no backoff for shared-NAT users hitting unauthenticated GitHub API limits.
attacks.evidence: 'a ~150-line Go service on the project's existing donated VPS'; ABSENT: load estimate, rate limit, or backoff.

attacks.claim: Recurring POST and update-check traffic on donated hardware has no bandwidth or storage budget, so 'no new paid infrastructure' is asserted rather than shown.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: bandwidth, storage, or quota budget for the collector VPS.

attacks.claim: Consent state is undefined when the prompt is interrupted by Ctrl-C or when the first post-upgrade run is non-interactive. It is unclear whether the prompt re-shows or the answer is recorded as declined.
attacks.evidence: 'On first interactive run after upgrade, kvx asks once'; ABSENT: persisted state and interrupt handling.

attacks.claim: The update notice and the consent prompt can fire on the same first invocation, and no ordering rule is specified. The bracketed [y/N] prompt also does not explain its default or the meaning of 'anonymous' for screen-reader users.
attacks.evidence: 'a single stderr line' and 'On first interactive run after upgrade, kvx asks once'; ABSENT: ordering rule and accessibility review.

attacks.claim: Monthly stats/ publication has no minimum cell size, so rare OS/arch and backend combinations could identify small deployments.
attacks.evidence: 'Aggregates are published monthly in the repo under stats/.'; ABSENT: minimum-count or suppression rule.

attacks.claim: The payload list is maintained in both code and docs/telemetry.md. The golden test checks the schema against the doc only, so the code can drift from what is actually sent.
attacks.evidence: 'golden test that the payload schema matches docs/telemetry.md'.

attacks.claim: Windows self-update support is not stated, despite the restriction on replacing a running executable. Only the telemetry service case is scoped out.
attacks.evidence: 'Telemetry for kvx running as a Windows service ... it stays off'; ABSENT: Windows self-update statement.

attacks.claim: The context cites two security fixes with slow uptake, but the motivation cites only the v2.6.3 fix.
attacks.evidence: Context: 'two security fixes this year had slow uptake'; Motivation: 'After the v2.6.3 credential-logging fix' only.

attacks.claim: The success measure depends on users running self-update, but the plan has no metric for notice-to-update conversion, so the team cannot tell whether the notice works.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: notice-to-update conversion metric.

attacks.claim: There is no acceptance test for raw-event deletion, although the 'raw events discarded' claim underpins the privacy story.
attacks.evidence: 'raw events discarded after aggregation'; ABSENT: test for raw-event deletion.
